common_name: Southern King Pear (Low-Chill Self-Fruitful Gulf Coast Pear)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Southern King needs only about 400 chill hours and is self-fruitful, making it a popular choice for home orchards around Houston and the Texas Gulf Coast.

directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Southern King is a low-chill Asian-European pear hybrid popular around Houston and the Gulf Coast of Texas, valued for reliable fruiting even after mild winters that leave higher-chill pears short on bloom, along with strong resistance to fire blight, the bacterial disease that devastates many European pear cultivars in humid Southern climates. It is self-fruitful, so a single tree will set fruit, though planting a second low-chill pear nearby can improve yields. Fruit is medium-sized with the sweet, mild flavor typical of Asian-pear influenced hybrids. Prune to an open, well-spaced framework to improve air circulation and further reduce fire blight risk, removing any blighted shoots promptly by cutting well below visible damage.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pear Variety Selection for Texas
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Pear Culture for the Gulf South
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Low-Chill Pear Production

common_name: Southern Queen Pear (Low-Chill Fire-Blight-Resistant Mississippi Pear)

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Southern Queen, selected in south Mississippi, needs a low chill requirement and is grown across the Gulf South for its excellent fire blight resistance.

directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Southern Queen, a low-chill pear selected in south Mississippi, is grown throughout the Gulf South for its large, bell-shaped fruit with russet-bronze skin and its excellent resistance to fire blight, the bacterial disease that limits many European pear cultivars in the region's warm, humid conditions. It ripens with the mild, sweet flavor typical of Southern low-chill pear selections and pairs well with a second low-chill pear nearby for improved cross-pollination and yield. Prune to an open, well-spaced framework to maximize air circulation, and cut out any fire blight-infected shoots promptly well below the visible damage to prevent the disease from spreading into older wood.
sources: Mississippi State University Extension — Pear Variety Recommendations
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Pear Culture for the Gulf South
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pear Variety Selection for Texas

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Baldwin, a Louisiana-origin pear, was selected for adaptability and fire blight resistance in Gulf South growing conditions.

directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun. Baldwin is a Louisiana-origin pear valued by Gulf South growers for its adaptability to the region's heat, humidity, and disease pressure, showing good resistance to fire blight, the bacterial disease that limits many higher-chill European pear cultivars in the Deep South. Like other regionally adapted low-chill pears it produces reliably even after a mild winter and pairs well with a second locally adapted pear cultivar for improved pollination and fruit set. Prune to an open, airy framework to reduce disease pressure, and remove any fire blight-infected shoots promptly, cutting well below visible damage into clean wood.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Pear Culture for the Gulf South
Mississippi State University Extension — Pear Variety Recommendations
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pear Variety Selection for Texas

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees in early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Magness is a USDA release famous for outstanding dessert flavor and strong fire blight resistance, but its pollen is sterile so it needs two other pear cultivars nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Plant bare-root trees in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, siting it near two other pear cultivars since Magness produces sterile pollen and cannot pollinate itself or other pears, though other pears can pollinate it. Magness is a USDA-released pear celebrated among fruit growers for its outstanding dessert quality, with smooth, buttery, exceptionally sweet flesh often ranked among the best-tasting of all pear cultivars, paired with strong resistance to fire blight that makes it a dependable choice for humid Southern growing conditions. Because of its sterile pollen, plant it alongside two compatible, fertile pear cultivars to ensure good fruit set on all three trees. Prune to an open framework for good air circulation, and remove any fire blight-infected shoots promptly, cutting well into clean wood below the damage.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Magness Pear Release Notes
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Pear Culture for the Gulf South
North Carolina State Extension — Pear Cultivars

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Byrongold, released in 1985 by the USDA research station in Byron, Georgia, was bred for improved disease tolerance under the heavy fungal and bacterial pressure of the humid Southeast.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, fertile soil in full sun, siting a second compatible Japanese plum nearby for cross-pollination and best fruit set. Byrongold was released in 1985 by the USDA-ARS research station in Byron, Georgia, from Ozark Premier breeding lines, selected specifically to hold up better against the disease pressure common in humid Southeastern orchards while producing round, yellow-fleshed fruit with good eating quality. Its Southeastern breeding background makes it a solid choice for Gulf South home orchards facing the fungal and bacterial diseases that trouble many plum cultivars developed for drier climates. Thin fruit if the tree sets heavily to improve size, and prune annually in late winter to maintain an open canopy that promotes airflow and reduces disease pressure.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service — Byron, Georgia Stone Fruit Breeding Program
University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Plum Variety Recommendations
Louisiana State University AgCenter — Plum Culture for the Gulf South
